title: The Snow Letters Mystery
markdown:
It started one nippy morning, the kind where the air tickles your nose and the world smells like frosty leaves. Luna the lemur, whose bright curious eyes missed nothing and whose tail wiggled with every new idea, was exploring Farmer Giles’s big farm. She was always ready for an adventure—sometimes a little too ready—which is why she was often first to spot anything out of the ordinary. Today her sharp gaze landed on the wide sloping roof of the old barn. Winter had dusted the shingles with a thick layer of snow, as if a baker had shaken sugar over everything. But the patches were not just drifts. They were forming funny shapes. Not fluffy clumps—letters. Big white letters, stark against the grey shingles.

Luna’s body buzzed. Her tail gave an extra-vigorous twitch. “Ooh, shapes!” she chirped. If something was interesting, Luna believed it was meant to be collected. She scrambled up the side of the barn, quick as a flash, paws finding every crevice and bump. She reached toward the nearest letter, a bold L. As soon as she touched it, a chill seeped into her fur. Then, in a blink, it was gone. Vanished, like mist. Only a damp patch remained. That was definitely not how collecting usually worked.

These were not just any snow letters. They were melting. Some stood big and clear. Others were faint smudges, like whispered secrets. They seemed to be disappearing in a certain order. A puzzle, forming right before her eyes.

That was when Crispin poked his long nose out of the pantry door. His scales shimmered a dusty purple, like a forgotten jewel. Crispin was a cupboard dragon, small enough to fit in a sturdy boot, with wise eyes as if he had read a million books. He lived in Farmer Giles’s pantry, a cozy kingdom of jars and sacks. “Luna, my friend,” he rumbled, voice like dry leaves after a long nap. “Those are not scribbles. Those are old signs.”

Luna skidded to a halt on the roof. “Signs? Like for a picnic, saying over here?”

Crispin chuckled, a puff of warm air that smelled of cinnamon and old paper. “Not quite. These are snow letters. And they are melting in a pattern. A pattern that means something very important.”

A gust whipped around the barn. It howled and tugged, snatching a few more letters and scattering them like tiny white birds. The sun peeked from behind a cloud, a little brighter, a little warmer. The letters shrank, edges turning to water. They were disappearing fast.

“We have to figure this out,” Luna exclaimed, her playful bounce replaced by a determined wiggle.

Crispin tapped a claw against his chin. He remembered snippets Farmer Giles had mentioned. “His grandfather told him stories. About monks. And bells.”

Monks and bells? Luna tilted her head. What did monks and their bells have to do with melting snow on a barn roof? She looked at the letters again. An L, then an I, then a G, then an H, then a T. That spelled Light. Then another L, and an O, and a T. “Lightlot?” she mumbled. It did not sound like much of anything.

Crispin closed his eyes, picturing the old monastery that used to stand on the hill overlooking the farm, now worn stones and ancient memories. “The monks did not have clocks with hands that tick and tock. They rang bells to mark the hours. The first bell for dawn, the next for mid-morning, and so on. Each bell had its own chime, its own time, its own sound.”

Luna’s eyes widened. The big clear letters were melting slowest, edges sharp and bright. The fainter ones, already giving up, were melting faster. “The older ones are melting slower,” she gasped. “Like the bells that rang first are still strong and clear, and the ones that rang later are fading.” It was not about collecting letters anymore. They were reading time itself.

The sun climbed. The air grew warmer. The barn roof felt like a toasted marshmallow under their paws. The letters—L, I, G, H, T, L, O, T—were almost puddles. The last few were faint whispers of white. They knew the letters related to time, but the meaning of the whole message remained a frustrating mystery.

Crispin shivered, not from chill but from the thrill of the puzzle. “There was one bell. The loudest. The one that meant the end of the day. The deepest chime. The most important of all.”

Luna wracked her brain, tail doing a thoughtful swish. She remembered Crispin’s cupboard. Sometimes, when the wind blew just right and the old house settled, a faint deep bong seemed to come from deep within the pantry. Not a bell, exactly, but a similar echoing sound—the sound of old things still keeping time.

“The bong!” Luna cried, leaping up. “The deep chime! It is not only the letters themselves. It is the order of the chimes, and which ones are the strongest.”

She remembered the sequence: L, I, G, H, T, L, O, T. Crispin remembered the bell sequence. The oldest bells, the first chimes, made the most solid clear letters. The youngest, the last chimes, made the faintest. The deep bong was last to ring, marking the final moments of the day.

“The last letter!” Luna shouted, scanning the roof. Almost gone, a faint smear of white, barely visible. But there it was. A capital S, so faint she might have missed it entirely if she had not been looking for the last one.

“S!” they both exclaimed. Lightlot S. A jumbled word. A secret code.

Then Crispin whispered, hushed with sudden insight, “Farmer Giles has a special box in the barn. He calls it his Story Box. He told me it holds his favourite tales. Tales that light up his world.”

Luna’s heart gave a little leap. She raced to the barn door, Crispin right behind, scales clattering softly. Beneath the eaves, near where the last faintest snow letter had been, stood a worn wooden chest, darkened with age. Carved into the lid, almost invisible from years of dust and wear, was a single faded S.

With a heave they pushed the lid open. Inside, nestled on soft faded velvet, were piles of old storybooks with colourful pictures—grand adventures, talking animals, daring quests, laughter bubbling from the pages. And at the very bottom, not gold or a glittering jewel, but a single perfect glistening snowball, as white and pure as the letters that had first appeared on the roof. Cold and perfect. A tiny echo of the mystery.

The treasure was not gold. It was stories themselves, a treasure that could be shared again and again. The snow letters had melted, leaving the warmth of a solved puzzle and the promise of countless tales. They sat down among the books, set the perfect snowball beside them, and began the most exciting tale they could find, their laughter echoing in the old barn. That is how Luna and Crispin found the best treasure of all—a whole box of adventures, just waiting to be opened.
